title: Many Qubits
intro: What changes when there is more than one qubit: the state space is a tensor product that grows as $2^n$, states can be entangled, a part of a system must be described by a density matrix, an environment makes superpositions fade, and the interactions between spins define the Hamiltonians quantum reservoirs are made of. This guide gives the order to read the seven pages in, what each teaches and the key equations.

blocks.text: What this chapter is about

Everything before this chapter was about one quantum system at a time: one qubit, one spin, one oscillator. A quantum reservoir is not like that. It is a register of qubits that interact, and the interesting behaviour lives in what several qubits can do together and in what you see when you can only look at part of them. This chapter takes you from the single qubit to that setting. It is the last chapter of the shelf, and its pages are the ones the QRC shelf leans on most heavily.

Three ideas run through it. First, the state space of several qubits is the tensor product of the individual spaces, so it grows as $2^n$ and contains states, entangled ones, that are not a list of states of the individual qubits. Second, when you look at only part of such a system, its state is no longer a vector but a density matrix, and a pure state of the whole can look mixed to a part. Third, real systems are never alone: the environment watches them, and the result is decoherence. A reservoir is built to live between these ideas, with interactions strong enough to mix information and an environment (or a reset) that makes it forget.
The order to read it in, and what each page teaches

items: Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems): how two systems are described together. Kronecker products built entry by entry, the basis order used by every simulator, how to write an operator that acts on one qubit of many, and why $n$ qubits need $2^n$ amplitudes.

Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement): states of two qubits that cannot be written as a product. A test for product states, the four Bell states and the Hadamard-plus-CNOT circuit that makes them, the Schmidt decomposition, the entanglement entropy that measures how entangled a pure state is, and why entanglement cannot be shared freely (monogamy).

The Partial Trace and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/partial-trace): what you get when you ignore one qubit. The reduced density matrix derived from measurement statistics and computed step by step for a product state, a Bell state and a partly entangled state, why a perfectly known pair can leave each half completely random, purity as a test for entanglement, and the partial trace in numpy.

Bell Inequalities and Nonlocality (#/quantum/many-body/bell-inequalities): why no model in which each particle carries pre-set answers can reproduce entanglement. The CHSH inequality derived, its local limit of 2, the quantum value $2\sqrt2$ computed with worked numbers, what the experiments of 1982 to 2015 showed, and why none of this allows faster-than-light signalling.

Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states): the density matrix as the description of a system you only partly know or only partly see: ignorance versus superposition, what makes a matrix a valid state, purity, the maximally mixed state, the Bloch ball, different ensembles with the same $\rho$, and how $\rho$ evolves and is measured. Every reservoir simulation on the QRC shelf starts from a mixed state.

Decoherence: How Superpositions Fade (#/quantum/many-body/decoherence): how a superposition fades when a qubit becomes entangled with its environment. Dephasing worked out for one and then many environment qubits, the dephasing and amplitude-damping channels with $T_1$ and $T_2$, measurement as decoherence, and the link to the Lindblad equation of the QRC shelf's open-systems chapter.

Spin Models (#/quantum/many-body/spin-models): the Hamiltonians that coupled qubits obey. Ising, transverse-field Ising, XX, XXZ and Heisenberg models built as matrices, two spins solved by hand, the quantum phase transition of the transverse-field Ising chain, and the random all-to-all Fujii-Nakajima reservoir Hamiltonian with its level statistics and the cost of simulating it.

blocks.text: Read them in this order, because each page uses the one before. If you are short of time, the pages the QRC shelf cannot do without are composite systems, the partial trace, mixed states, decoherence and spin models; entanglement and Bell inequalities explain why reduced states behave as they do, and are what make the rest feel like physics instead of bookkeeping (the partial-trace page needs only the product test and the Bell states from the entanglement page).
What you need first

The chapter assumes the Foundations chapter (Foundations (#/quantum/foundations)), the Bloch sphere and Pauli operators from Qubits (#/quantum/qubits), and the Schrödinger equation $U = e^{-iHt}$ from Dynamics (#/quantum/dynamics). In particular you should be comfortable with kets and bras, the Born rule, Pauli matrices, and reading a matrix such as $e^{-iHt}$. The symmetries page of the Dynamics chapter is useful before the spin-models page.
How long it takes

There are seven pages. Allowing about two hours a page if you work the examples and the problems (an estimate, not a measurement) the chapter takes roughly 14 hours, spread over a week or two. A reading-only pass without problems is about half that. The partial-trace and mixed-state pages repay slow reading: reduced states are the single hardest idea in the chapter and the rest of the QRC shelf uses it on every page.
The key equations of the chapter

What it means: two systems together have as many amplitudes as the product of their sizes, so 10 qubits have $1024$ and 50 qubits have about $1.1\times10^{15}$. This growth is both the promise of quantum computing and the reason that classical simulation fails.

blocks.caption: A Bell state, the simplest entangled state.

blocks.text: What it means: neither qubit has a state of its own, yet the two results of measuring them in the same basis always agree. It cannot be written as $\vert\alpha\rangle\otimes\vert\beta\rangle$.

blocks.caption: The reduced state of part A: sum over the part you ignore.

blocks.text: What it means: the best description of one part of a larger system. For $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$ it is $I/2$, completely mixed, although the whole is pure.

blocks.tex: S = E(a, b) + E(a, b') + E(a', b) - E(a', b'),\qquad \vert S\vert\le2\ \text{(local models)},\qquad S_{\text{quantum}} = 2\sqrt2\approx2.83
blocks.caption: The CHSH quantity: E is the correlation of the two results for detector settings a or a' and b or b'.

blocks.text: What it means: any theory in which measurement results are fixed in advance by local hidden variables keeps $\vert S\vert$ at or below 2; a Bell state measured at the right angles reaches $2.83$, and experiments agree with quantum mechanics.

blocks.caption: The density matrix and its purity.

blocks.text: What it means: $\rho$ describes a probabilistic mixture of pure states; the purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$ equals 1 for a pure state and $1/d$ for the maximally mixed state of dimension $d$ (so $1/2$ for one qubit).

blocks.caption: The transverse-field Ising chain and the Fujii-Nakajima reservoir Hamiltonian.

blocks.text: What it means: a spin model is a sum of fields and couplings. The first competes order against fluctuation and has a phase transition at $h = J$; the second, with random coefficients on every pair, is generic and conserves only the parity $\prod Z_i$.
One thing to keep in mind

Conventions are fixed across the chapter and the QRC shelf: $\vert0\rangle$ has $Z = +1$, the leftmost factor of a tensor product is qubit 1, the basis is ordered $00, 01, 10, 11$, $H$ is the Hamiltonian and $H_d$ the Hadamard gate, and $\hbar = 1$. A wrong guess about the qubit order is the most common reason a hand calculation disagrees with a simulator.
Where to go next

The topic that continues this chapter's story on the Quantum Reservoir Computing shelf (Quantum Reservoir Computing (#/qrc)) is Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems), which picks up density matrices and decoherence and turns them into the channels and Lindblad equations that describe a dissipative reservoir. The reservoir Hamiltonian itself is on The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir).
